blocks.value: An interface specifies method headings that any implementing class must provide, without saying how they work. A class implements one or more interfaces:

public class ClassName implements InterfaceName1, InterfaceName2 { }

public class Rectangle implements Countable, Measurable { }
An abstract class can't be instantiated directly, only subclassed. It can mix regular methods with abstract methods, which are methods declared but not implemented:

public abstract class ClassName { }

public abstract void methodName();
Interfaces and abstract classes are similar (neither can be instantiated), but they solve different problems.

Favor an interface when unrelated classes need to share a contract, when you care about the behavior a type exposes rather than who implements it, or when you want a type to combine multiple sets of required behavior.

Favor an abstract class when you want to share actual code among closely related classes, when subclasses are expected to have many fields or methods in common, or when you need non-public access modifiers or non-static/non-final fields.
